title: If You Turned 16 in 1960, This Was Your Freedom

scenes.text: In nineteen sixty, turning sixteen was the biggest birthday of all. Bigger than eighteen, bigger than twenty-one. Because at sixteen, in most of America, you could get a driver's license. And a driver's license meant one thing. Freedom. The freedom to go anywhere, with anyone, any time you could talk your father into handing over the keys.
scenes.caption: SIXTEEN

scenes.text: If you turned sixteen in nineteen sixty, you were born in nineteen forty-four, during the last full year of the Second World War. Your father might have been overseas when you were born. You grew up in the boom years of the fifties. And now, at sixteen, the whole country seemed to be waiting for you.
scenes.caption: BORN IN 1944

scenes.text: So let's look at what turning sixteen in nineteen sixty really meant. The license, the first car, the first job, the first real date, and all the little freedoms that came with them. If that was you, get ready to feel sixteen again.
scenes.caption: ALL THE LITTLE FREEDOMS

scenes.text: In nineteen sixty, there were about ten million Americans between the ages of fifteen and seventeen, and the number was climbing every year as the baby boom grew up. Car makers, record companies, soft drink brands and clothing stores were all chasing them. Being sixteen had never mattered so much to so many people.
scenes.caption: 10 MILLION TEENAGERS

scenes.text: It started with driver's education. By nineteen sixty, most high schools offered a driver's ed class, often taught by the gym teacher or the football coach. There was classroom time, with a thick rule book and films about safe driving. And then there was the car.
scenes.caption: DRIVER'S ED

scenes.text: The school's training car was usually a big sedan donated by a local dealer, with the school's name painted on the side. It had a second brake pedal on the passenger's side, for the teacher. Three or four students rode along, waiting their turn, and watching their classmates grind the gears and stall at stop signs.
scenes.caption: THE SECOND BRAKE PEDAL

scenes.text: Those safety films were famous for being terrifying. Movies with titles like Signal Thirty and Mechanized Death showed real car crashes, with real victims, to scare teenagers into driving carefully. Many people who sat through them in the late fifties and early sixties say they still remember every frame.
scenes.caption: THE SCARY FILMS

scenes.text: Then came the big day. The driving test. You went to the motor vehicle office with your father, who was probably more nervous than you were. You took a written test, an eye test, and then sat in the car with a stern examiner holding a clipboard. Parallel parking was the part everyone dreaded.
scenes.caption: THE DRIVING TEST

scenes.text: Most cars in nineteen sixty had a manual transmission, or a column shift on the steering wheel. No power steering in many of them, so parallel parking took real muscle. Turn signals were standard by then, but many drivers still used hand signals out the window. Arm straight out for left, arm up for right, arm down for stop.
scenes.caption: HAND SIGNALS

scenes.text: When you passed, you got a paper license, with no photo in most states. You folded it into your wallet and checked it a hundred times. That night, you asked your father for the keys. And the answer, often, was not yet. But eventually, he gave in.
scenes.caption: THE PAPER LICENSE

scenes.text: Of course, many teenagers had been driving long before sixteen. On farms, kids drove tractors and pickup trucks at ten or twelve. In the country, a fourteen-year-old might drive to the feed store for his father. In some states, farm kids could get a special license at fourteen. For them, sixteen was just making it official.
scenes.caption: FARM KIDS DROVE AT TWELVE

scenes.text: Most sixteen-year-olds in nineteen sixty didn't have their own car. They borrowed the family car. And that came with rules. Be home by eleven. No more than three friends. Don't go over fifty. Fill it up with gas before you bring it back. And don't you dare put a scratch on it.
scenes.caption: THE RULES

scenes.text: The family car might be a big Chevy Impala, a Ford Fairlane or a Plymouth Fury. In nineteen sixty, those cars had huge tailfins, lots of chrome and bench seats front and back. Teenagers loved the bench seats, because a girl could slide right over next to the boy who was driving.
scenes.caption: THE TAILFINS

scenes.text: Many fathers checked the odometer when the car came back. If you'd gone sixty miles to a drive-in that was only five miles away, there were questions. Clever teenagers learned which back roads added the fewest miles.
scenes.caption: HE CHECKED THE ODOMETER

scenes.text: The real dream was a car of your own. And in nineteen sixty, it was possible. An old used car, like a nineteen forty-nine Ford or a nineteen fifty Chevy, might cost a hundred or two hundred dollars. A teenage boy with a summer job could save that in a few months.
scenes.caption: A $150 CAR

scenes.text: That first car was usually a wreck. Rust holes in the floor. A radio that only got one station. Tires as bald as an egg. But to a sixteen-year-old, it was the most beautiful thing in the world. Boys spent every spare hour and every dollar on it, washing it, waxing it, and working on the engine in the driveway.
scenes.query: 1960 teenage boys working on car engine
scenes.caption: THE MOST BEAUTIFUL THING

scenes.text: Then came the customizing. Boys lowered their cars, painted flames on the hood, and added loud glasspack mufflers. They hung fuzzy dice from the rearview mirror, put on a suicide knob for one-handed steering, and installed a reverb unit for the radio. Hot rod magazines showed them how. Every car told you something about the boy who drove it.
scenes.caption: FUZZY DICE

scenes.text: Gasoline cost about thirty-one cents a gallon in nineteen sixty. A dollar's worth would get you through a weekend of cruising. Teenagers often pooled their change to buy gas, a quarter here and a dime there. Fill it with two dollars was a common order at the pump.
scenes.caption: A DOLLAR'S WORTH

scenes.text: Paying for that car meant a job. At sixteen, you could legally work most jobs, and teenagers were everywhere. Boys pumped gas, bagged groceries, flipped burgers, caddied at the golf course, and worked on farms and construction crews in the summer. Girls babysat, worked at the five-and-dime, the drugstore or the movie theater, and waited tables.
scenes.caption: THE FIRST JOB

scenes.text: The minimum wage in nineteen sixty was a dollar an hour, though many teen jobs paid less. Your first paycheck came in a little envelope, or as cash. The first thing many teenagers did was get a Social Security card, with their number typed on it, and they memorized that number for the rest of their lives.
scenes.caption: THE SOCIAL SECURITY CARD

scenes.text: A job meant more than money. It meant responsibility, and being treated like an adult. A boss who expected you on time. Customers who didn't care that you were sixteen. Many people say they learned more at their first job than in a whole year of school.
scenes.caption: TREATED LIKE AN ADULT

scenes.text: And money meant buying things for yourself, for the first time. A new pair of jeans or a sweater from the department store. Records, at about a dollar for a forty-five. A transistor radio, which by nineteen sixty was small enough for a shirt pocket. Tickets to a concert. And a class ring, which cost about thirty dollars and was a very big deal.
scenes.caption: YOUR OWN MONEY

scenes.text: With a car and a little money came the first real date. Not a group trip to the soda fountain, but a real date. You called her on the family phone, with your little brother listening. You asked her father's permission. On Saturday night, you washed the car, put on a clean shirt and a splash of your father's aftershave.
scenes.caption: THE PHONE CALL

scenes.text: You picked her up at her front door. You talked to her father for five very long minutes. Then off to the drive-in, the movie theater downtown, or a school dance. Afterward, a burger and a shake at the drive-in restaurant, where a carhop on roller skates brought the tray right to your car window.
scenes.caption: THE CARHOP

scenes.text: And then the drive home, as slowly as possible, with the radio playing. In nineteen sixty, the songs were Elvis's It's Now or Never, Percy Faith's Theme from A Summer Place, the Everly Brothers' Cathy's Clown, and Chubby Checker's The Twist. And she had to be home by eleven. Her father was watching from the window.
scenes.caption: THE THEME FROM A SUMMER PLACE

scenes.text: If things went well, there was a second date, and a third. Then maybe going steady, which meant a class ring on a chain, or a letter jacket draped over her shoulders. Couples went steady for months, or for years. And many sixteen-year-olds of nineteen sixty married their high school sweethearts a few years later.
scenes.caption: GOING STEADY

scenes.text: On Friday and Saturday nights, sixteen-year-olds went cruising. Every town had a strip, the main street or a highway at the edge of town. Teenagers drove slowly up and down, again and again, windows down, radios up, waving to friends, honking at girls, and looking for a party.
scenes.caption: CRUISING THE STRIP

scenes.text: The drive-in restaurant was the center of it all. A&W, Bob's Big Boy, or a local place with a neon sign. Cars circled the lot, showing off. Boys revved their engines. Sometimes, out on a quiet stretch of road, two cars lined up for a drag race, which was illegal, dangerous and very, very exciting.
scenes.caption: THE DRIVE-IN

scenes.text: For the first time in history, teenagers could go places without their parents knowing exactly where they were. That freedom made parents nervous, and newspapers wrote worried stories about teenagers and their cars. But for sixteen-year-olds, it was the best feeling in the world.
scenes.caption: THE BEST FEELING IN THE WORLD

scenes.text: There were also some dangerous habits. Nobody wore seat belts, and many cars didn't even have them. Teenagers drove too fast, piled too many friends into the car, and raced on back roads. Car crashes were the leading cause of death for American teenagers. Almost every high school lost a student in a crash, and the whole town mourned.
scenes.caption: DANGEROUS HABITS

scenes.text: Turning sixteen in nineteen sixty also meant noticing the bigger world. That fall, there was a presidential election between John Kennedy and Richard Nixon, and for the first time, the candidates debated on television. Teenagers watched with their parents. Kennedy was young and handsome, and many teenagers felt like he spoke to them.
scenes.caption: KENNEDY VS NIXON

scenes.text: It was also the year of the Greensboro sit-ins, when young Black college students sat at a lunch counter and refused to leave. Many sixteen-year-olds, Black and white, watched the news and began to think about fairness and justice. Some would join the civil rights movement within a few years.
scenes.caption: GREENSBORO

scenes.text: And there was the future. Boys knew that the draft was waiting at eighteen. Girls knew they were expected to marry young, and many would be married by twenty. College was becoming more common. The sixteen-year-olds of nineteen sixty were about to graduate into a decade that would change everything.
scenes.caption: THE FUTURE

scenes.text: If you turned sixteen in nineteen sixty, you're in your early eighties now. You've driven dozens of cars since then. But I'd bet you still remember the first one. The color, the smell of the seats, the sound of the engine, and the feeling of driving away from home for the first time with nobody else in the car.
scenes.caption: THE FIRST ONE

scenes.text: That's what sixteen meant in nineteen sixty. Not just a license, but the start of becoming your own person. Making your own money. Making your own choices. And learning that freedom always comes with a few rules, usually written by your father.
scenes.caption: BECOMING YOUR OWN PERSON

scenes.text: So tell us in the comments. What was your first car, and how much did you pay for it? Where did you go on your first drive alone? What was your first job? We read every comment. Next time, we're looking at what every American family ate for dinner in nineteen fifty-eight. Thank you for spending this time with me.
scenes.caption: WHAT WAS YOUR FIRST CAR?
